# 1. 

## a.

$$
\text{Provided that}: \qquad \bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 0) = 1, \qquad \bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 0) = 5,
$$

$$
\bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 1) = 4, \qquad \bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 1) = 7
$$

> we can hold the following to be true.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 0) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 0, B = 0)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 0 + \beta_2 \cdot 0 + \beta_3 \cdot 0 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + 0 = 1\\
\therefore \beta_0 = 1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 0) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 1, B = 0)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 + \beta_2 \cdot 0 + \beta_3 \cdot 0 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 + 0 + 0 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= 1 + \beta_1 + 0 = 5\\
\therefore \beta_1 = 4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 1) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 0, B = 1)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 0 + \beta_2 \cdot 1 + \beta_3 \cdot 0 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + 0 + \beta_2 + 0 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= 1 + \beta_2 + 0 = 4\\
\therefore \beta_2 = 3
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 1) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 1, B = 1)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 + \beta_2 \cdot 1 + \beta_3 \cdot 1 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= 1 + 4 + 3 + \beta_3 = 7\\
\therefore \beta_3 = -1
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Final Answer**: $\boxed{\beta_0 = 1, \beta_1 = 4, \beta_2 = 3, \beta_3 = -1}$

## b. 

> In order to get estimates for the four regression coefficients, we need estimates for the four averages above. We have two variables, $A$ and $B$, which can take values $0$ or $1$ depending on whether or not the value observed was at a "high" or "low" level for each. $\beta_0$, the intercept or "baseline", necessitates that we have a treatment group where $A = 0, B=0$. Then, by comparing to our baseline, we can get our treatment effects for $A$ and $B$ by changing the level one at a time: one group is $A=1, B=0$, and the other $A = 0, B=1$. This lets us estimate $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$. We also have to estimate the interaction effect $\beta_3$, so we need treatment group $A = 1, B = 1$. This constructs our full factorial design, where we have $2^2$ treatment groups, one for each combination of treatment levels. Then, our observational units are evenly split among the treatment groups.

> In summary:

| Group | Treatment | Number of units |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
|Group 1| $A = 0, B = 0$ |$n=50$|
|Group 2| $A = 1, B = 0$ |$n=50$|
|Group 3| $A = 0, B = 1$ |$n=50$|
|Group 4| $A = 1, B = 1$ |$n=50$|
